NEXTDC chair says inner-city site "wouldn't happen again"
The M3 site in West Footscray has houses on multiple sides but has been an industrial site for 100 years.
It's already a data centre, but the community is opposed to the expansion occurring next door.
But asked about the problems with the site, chair Doug Flynn says the company wouldn't buy a site like that again.
"It wouldn't happen again," he said.
I'll paraphrase what he said further (because I was still standing at the microphone) but it was along the lines that 'it's not like it's been a playground for children'.
For some of those 100 years it has been a petrochemical site.
NEXTDC thanks its shareholders
NEXTDC CEO Craig Scroggie has just finished speaking.
There was no applause, although that's not uncommon in annual general meetings.
He ends by thanking shareholders in the data centre builder and operator:
"We started with one site in Brisbane. Today we operate 18.
"M3 (the contentious West Footscray expansion) is a serious setback. Solving it is our first priority, and we will see it through.
"We will work to earn back your trust and the trust of the community around M3.
"I will report to you on progress in February. Outside M3, the business is performing, and demand is the strongest I have seen. Our job is to deliver the value in this business for our shareholders.
"That is what we will do. Thank you."
NEXTDC developing 'engagement plan' after furore over data centre
So, what is NEXTDC doing about the communities it operates in, since it got an epic kicking from a community in inner Melbourne while trying to expand a data centre?
The M3 project smashed the share price by -42% in a day and led to a direct rival buying a tenth of the company at a bargain-basement price.
Here's a little of CEO Craig Scroggie, who is penitent about how the company has been behaving and how it needs to change.
"M3 has changed how we plan, build and operate alongside our neighbours.
"For more than 15 years we have built data centres across this country. What earned trust then is not enough now.
"Community expectations have moved in the age of AI, and we must move with them. At M3, we have reviewed our community engagement, and the findings are shaping a formal M3 Community Engagement Plan.

"We are establishing a Community Consultative Committee, a standing forum for residents and local stakeholders to raise issues with us directly. We are also developing a Community Engagement Plan for every site in Australia and in Asia.

"The Board oversees that work through its Sustainability Committee and two Board sponsors. We have launched a dedicated M3 website and contact channels and introduced defined response times for complaints and enquiries.
"We are providing more regular information on construction, generators and air quality. These standards apply to everyone who works on our sites, including our builders.

"Our company-wide approach is built around the five commitments on this slide (I'm in a room where a Powerport is also playing) engage early and listen, plan responsibly, respect our neighbours, show our progress, and create value that lasts".
NEXTDC CEO apologetic at 'hardest' AGM
Data centre firm NEXTDC CEO Craig Scroggie is now speaking, describing the AGM as his 15th as CEO, "and it is the hardest".

"We build on industrial land, close to power, network connectivity and our customers. In the past we relied on formal council and state planning processes to set the standard and own the conversation with the community.
"That is no longer enough. We will now engage earlier and directly, alongside our power and construction partners.

"First, some context. M3 is not a new development. It has been under development since 2021, in an industrial precinct in West Footscray. Stages 6 and 7 are the final stages of the entire campus. Over those years, community views on industrial areas have changed, and opposition to data centres and AI has grown, locally and globally. That is the environment we are now building in."
So, a little kick for councils and governments, but acknowledging that they dropped the ball.
NEXTDC to get 'second strike' and spill motion
Last year, investors said "NO!" to the remuneration report.
This action, called a 'first strike' and means that if there's a second one at the next annual general meeting, today, there can be a call for the board to be dumped.
That is happening today.
Here's chair Doug Flynn on an inevitable second strike.
"Our view on pay is that it should appropriately reflect the market given scarcity of talent and complexity, scale and the expansion of the business.
"We continue to evaluate remuneration to ensure it remains fit-for-purpose, rewards and retains critical talent and has strong pay-for-performance alignment.
"It is important to note that proxies lodged before today's meeting show 72.03%* of votes against the Remuneration Report.
"That means the Company will record a second strike today, and Resolution 8, the conditional spill resolution, will be put to the meeting.

"We strongly believe a spill meeting would be destabilising and add cost and distraction at exactly the time when the Board and management need to focus on delivering for all shareholders. The Board recommends that you vote against Resolution 8, and I intend to vote all available undirected proxies against it."
* This is the result of votes before the meeting. A vote of 25% or more is enough, so this is happening.
NEXTDC AGM underway
Veteran data centre operator NEXTDC has had quite a year.
The environment around data centres has changed massively. Protests in Europe and the US translated into major wins for anti-data-centre politicians and proposals.
A small community protest about powerpoles snowballed into the share price getting smashed -42% in a day.
The low price led to a corporate raid by a competitor, who now own almost 10% of it.
NEXTDC's annual general meeting for shareholders is just getting underway. The meeting has been moved to a Sydney CBD hotel due to demand for seats.
Outgoing chair Doug Flynn has just started speaking.
"[There is] growing community opposition to data centres ... we do not intend to pursue new development opportunities that are near residential areas," he says.
You can read more about the problems facing NEXTDC here. I'll keep blogging from the meeting

UBS: Rates have peaked, but growing earnings risks mean it's still too early for the full 'pivot trade'

Australian interest rates may have peaked, but growing signs of weakness in the economy mean investors should be cautious about piling into retailers and banks, according to Richard Schellbach, Equity Strategist of UBS.
In a research note, he pointed to a sharp deterioration in the labour market, with employment falling by 44,000 in October and the unemployment rate jumping to 4.9%, its highest level since 2021.

''Worryingly, these October numbers don’t capture the cuts many high-profile businesses have made to their staffing numbers over recent weeks, nor the impact from the 25bp hike the RBA put through just two weeks ago."

While UBS economists have brought forward their forecast for the RBA’s first interest rate cut from November to August 2027, Richard cautioned against rushing into stocks that typically benefit from falling rates.
''It seems clear now that 'peak rates' have been seen, with our economists bringing forward their first rate cut to Aug-27, was previously Nov-27.
A 'rate pivot' trade to buy the domestic consumer / housing cyclicals would seem tempting… but we would caution given the risks of more significant earnings downgrades are now building.
We also note that a rising unemployment rate has long been associated with a loss of earnings momentum to the sectors most exposed to the domestic consumer / housing complex.”

Data centre operator NEXTDC raises annual forecast on sales growth and cost savings

NEXTDC has raised its fiscal 2027 net revenue and underlying operating earnings forecast, reflecting strong sales and revenue growth outside the affected M3 contracts, as well as cost-saving measures.
The data centre operator expects annual net revenue of $485 million to $500 million, up from its previous guidance of $475 million to $500 million.

Full-year underlying earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation are projected to be between $260 million and $275 million, compared with its previous guidance of $245 million to $265 million.
The company will hold its AGM today.

Morningstar sees upside in Anthropic despite risks from fierce AI competition

Morningstar senior equity market strategist Lochlan Halloway has issued a note saying Anthropic shares are marginally undervalued, with a fair value estimate of $US92, compared with its $US83 IPO price.
But the research firm draws comparisons with the textile and fibre-optic industries, where heavy investment and fierce competition drove down prices and undermined profitability.
''A leading model has only a few months to earn enough to pay for its successor, and each successor has so far cost more to build,'' the note says.
Despite those risks, Halloway remains optimistic about Anthropic’s prospects.
''We think Anthropic can avoid that fate.
''Each generation of its models helps build the next, and long-term deals for computing power let it train them more cheaply than most competitors.
"And as each generation costs more to build, fewer labs can afford to keep up.”
''The prize is large: the newest models have launched at the highest prices yet, and customers have paid, because a better answer is worth more to them.
We expect Anthropic to stay at the frontier for at least the next decade, which underpins our narrow moat rating.”

Morningstar forecasts annual revenue growth of around 50% over the next five years, but warns that the range of potential outcomes remains very wide, with a bull-case valuation of $US188 a share and a bear case of just $US25.

Our bear case, at US$25, is a world where the frontier stalls. If building bigger models stops producing much better ones, rivals catch up, the free open models become good enough for most businesses, and the premium Anthropic charges fades. That is the dark fibre outcome.

What does Anthropic's blockbuster IPO mean for the AI trade? We ask analysts
I've been speaking to market analysts about their thoughts on this topic. Here are some thoughts:
Daniel Newman, chief executive of US technology research firm Futurum Group, said the broader AI industry still faced some difficult questions despite Anthropic's record float.
He pointed to high interest rates, persistent inflation and geopolitical uncertainty weighing on technology stocks, even as demand for AI continues to grow.
"Nvidia's strong earnings didn't save the AI trade. Anthropic's IPO probably won't save it either," he said.
Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com:

Anthropic's IPO signals continued bullishness about artificial intelligence. In particular, this is a show of confidence in the growth and innovation promised by AI technology - and specifically, a company that will be responsible for driving much of that growth and innovation.
However, the risks to the AI sector won't be assuaged by this IPO alone. Investors are worried about a peak in the investment boom and more moderate profit growth in the future from AI companies.

On top of that, macro risks relating to persistent inflationary pressures and higher interest rates - something the AI boom is contributing to -are also weighing on market sentiment as traders price in the possibility of a 50 basis point rate hike from the Fed next month.

Aussie demand for Anthropic shares strong, say market analysts
Australian investors were among a select group outside the United States given the opportunity to buy shares in Anthropic before its stock market debut.
Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said his firm's grey market indicators had pointed to a strong debut for Anthropic.
The indicator allows traders to speculate on a company's share price before it officially hits the stock exchange, providing an early indication of investor expectations.
"If you sort of use that as a rough guide, demand's been really strong," he said.
Mr Rodda compared the excitement to the launch of a new iPhone.
"People lining up around the streets to be some of the first people to get their hands on it," he said."It's very, very much a similar sort of psychology dynamic amongst investors."

Wall Street falls despite Anthropic's strong debut
Despite a surging start for Anthropic on debut, US stocks fell, it seems investors remained cautious about the sector’s outlook.
All three major Wall Street indexes retreated, with the S&P 500 heading for its fifth consecutive session of losses.

Jun Bei Liu from Ten Cap told me this morning said she had expected Anthropic’s strong debut to help revive the AI trade, but the broader market reaction suggested investors remained concerned about valuations.

''I thought it might revive the AI trade somewhat, given its strong listing. But it seems it’s failed to do so,'' she said.''It certainly seems like there’s enough demand, but the price is still too high.''
''I thought it might revive the AI trade somewhat, given its strong listing. But it seems it’s failed to do so,'' she said.
''It certainly seems like there’s enough demand, but the price is still too high.''
Dan Ives says Anthropic debut could help restore confidence in the AI trade

Prominent tech bull Dan Ives, of Yorkville Ives, says in a note this morning that Anthropic’s blockbuster Wall Street debut could help restore investor confidence in the AI sector, despite the recent turbulence in technology stocks.

''At a time in which investors are very nervous on the overall tech trade and the Nvidia black cloud moment casts a shadow over the tech sector, Anthropic’s debut is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,'' he said.

''It is going through a very turbulent, white-knuckle period that does not change our longer-term view that $3 trillion to $4 trillion of capex will be spent over the next few years on the AI Revolution, and this sets the stage for the next phase of tech and infrastructure investment with Anthropic a central player in the buildout.''

Ives said the listing gives investors an opportunity to assess a frontier AI developer as a publicly traded company, with its financial performance and enormous computing commitments now under greater scrutiny.
Key Event
Anthropic hit the Nasdaq running
Shares in Anthropic have surged in their Wall Street debut, briefly pushing the artificial intelligence company’s market value above $US2 trillion ($3 trillion) overtaking SpaceX debut.

The maker of the Claude AI chatbot opened at $US111.50 ($167) on the Nasdaq, a 34 per cent jump from its initial public offering price of $US83, as investors rushed to buy into the first major frontier AI company to list on a stock exchange.
The blockbuster debut marked a major milestone for the AI inudstry, but the initial excitment faded as investors took profits and its shares gave up some of its early gains.
The main US indexes also retreated amid renewed jitters over the sector's outlook. The stock, trading under the ticker 'ANT' was last quoted at $US96.30, as at 7 am AEDT.
Anthropic raised $US81.3 billion through its IPO, alongside a further $26US billion in a concurrent private placement involving major technology companies.

The listing comes at a turbulent time for the technology sector, which has been rattled by concerns of an AI bubble, worries over mounting debt among data centre operators and a widening scandal that forced Nvidia founder Jensen Huang to step down as CEO.

Anthropic: What we know
So here's what we know about Anthropic listing.
It was shaping up to be one of the initial public offerings in history.
It will trade under the ticker symbol ANT
It was mooted to list at $83 with others valuing it was $70 to $78, but listed at a whopping $111.51 some 34 per cent higher than expected.
This puts the total value of the listing at about more than $2 trillion.
It raised more than $81 billion dollars, making it the largest fundraiser in history and eclipsed SpaceX's $75 billion.
Chief executive Dario Amodei rang the bell to open the Nasdaq to mark its launch.
He's planning to sell about $260m worth of shares that could make him worth $18 billion.
It's the maker of Claude, a large language model (LLM), popular with businesses globally.
